p: [interposing] Per year. Per year.

Per Year. Would like to walk back to Mr. McCarthy. Is it fair to say that free buses could mean slower buses? And would that— you think that would— would that be something that would remain consistent?

It– look, there's— I don't know that that's— that it means slower, but the New York Times did it. They sent out a bunch of reporters and they did a, you know, a pretty thorough look at a bus route, and they determined that the speed gained from not having someone pay was— or the time it took for someone to pay was not the issue for the pace of buses. It was the congestion on the roads. It was double-parked cars. It was the lack of

enforcement in many areas. So, that's, you know, that's something that I know you and others are focused on, and it makes a lot of sense. Based on what they reported out.
Not to make headlines, Mr. Chairman, would you say fast and free are contradictory?
No comment.
Okay.

I think the point is we're ready to do— we're working with the city to do fast. That is under— that discussion is well underway, and I credit the new DOT team and the mayor and the mayor's team for stepping up on that. So let's get going and doing fast. We have a lot of questions relevant to the second half of that sentence.
I think I know your answer on this one. Does the MTA support trialing free buses again during the World Cup?
I haven't— honestly, I haven't been asked that by anybody in a position.
Okay.
And we're not at— we're not going to study things that are not on, you know, not on the agenda of the city and the state and other power players.
Has the city or state asked you to do anything on this?
No. No. Nobody's asked me to give free buses to–
[interposing] Okay.
people who are paying $1,000 a ticket from other countries. No one's asked me that so far.

Fair, fair. A city comptroller report from September 2025 found a majority of buses are performing at below average standards. 56 percent of bus lines, 186 out of 332, received a grade of D or lower, meaning that they run at speeds significantly below the borough-wide average, are more likely to experience bunching and consistently fail to arrive at scheduled stops on time. By comparison, only 27 lines, eight percent, received a B or higher. Only seven lines received an A grade per hour, consistent with January 2019 speeds

at 7.8 miles per hour. What is the MTA doing to improve bus speeds throughout the city?

Okay, so you've just made– recited stats that are the most powerful argument for all of this bus speed initiatives that have been the law of the— some of them have been the law of the City of New York for several years but haven't been implemented.
Talking about the Streets Plan?
I'm talking about the street—
We have a hearing on that later. I'm going to zero in on it.

Okay, so we're for all of those initiatives. Well, we are strong supporters of the busway goals, the bus lane goals, including potentially busways. We're strong support. We have been pushing, pushing for more and more ACE cameras, and ACE cameras are a success. We have seen improvements in speed on those routes. We have seen consistent improvements in speed. We have seen that people don't violate again and again and again. Give New Yorkers credit, just like they are where there

are speed cameras, when they know that there are ACE cameras there, they are not engaged in, you know, repetitive recidivist violations. So the system is working where we get– where we get the ACE cameras. And that's at eight over— I think how many routes? It's a huge— I'll get you the number, but it's— but a huge portion of our routes, about 20 percent of our routes now are now covered by ACE cameras. We want more traffic enforcement agents to break the bottlenecks, but we have been supporters of, you know, traffic signal prioritization, which is another DOT initiative. And the whole congestion pricing initiative was obviously focused on trying to make buses move more closely. And we have engaged in these borough-by-borough bus network redesigns. I'm not going to give you all the details, but you know we have been leaders in trying to make buses faster using all these techniques, and we're going to continue to push forward, especially now that we have a partner, hopefully, in the city

And Chair, if I could just add to that, we have been— you know, Commissioner Flynn's team has been meeting with us, and they're, you know, very enthusiastic and working

together on ways that we can make buses faster. And this really getting into the nitty-gritty, including the bus lanes, including enforcement, and really the MTA looking at themselves and how we can run buses out of depots faster, whether it's signalization and other things. So this is a— it's a good time for anyone interested in faster buses, because I think the teams are really working well together.

Collaboration is great, and we'd love to see, you know, more of that. I have a follow-up to ACE Program. A lot of these cameras— the cameras capture the back of the cars, but at what point are they going to start capturing the front of the cars? Because you— we find a lot of folks– in my neck of the woods, they cover the license plates in the back, or they'll put the hood, of their car up so you don't capture it. Are we working on technology to also capture the front of the cars?

Yeah, but I'll just say that, you know, the pattern of folks covering license plates, altering license plates. I mean, you know, one thing that the last administration got right is that messing with license plates is a crime issue in

New York. It's not just an MTA bus lane enforcement issue. People messing with license plates is very deeply connected to the crime issues in New York. And I'm hoping and confident that the— under the new administration, the police will continue to enforce on that because that is a huge problem.
What has been the impact of congestion pricing on bus speeds, if any?

There has been improvement, although it's– you know, I have to check that— there has been an improvement. The greatest improvement is obviously this— the buses that are moving the fastest are the express bus buses that are coming into the city by— on the crossings. So you have the Holland and the Lincoln Tunnel. The Holland Tunnel, you're 50 percent reduction in the time to get across. Lincoln Tunnel was like 30 percent. The Williamsburg Bridge and other East River crossings have also seen significant improvements in speed. So express buses and the inter— intra-borough buses coming to Manhattan, dramatic improvements. In Manhattan itself, the improvements in speed have been somewhat less, but they are also– they've also been

validated and documented, and we'll provide those details. John, do you have anything on that?

Bus speeds are up, but not as much as the other vehicle speeds entering the zone, where, as the Chair said, is where we're seeing the most dramatic increase. There are other reasons that will slow down a bus within the zone, again, going back into the idea of how cars are parked and, and how traffic is moving once you're inside the zone. So, but we have seen increase in speed— bus speeds within the zone.
I'm now going to turn over to my colleagues, Council Member Lynn Schulman.

Thank you very much, and thank you for being here. I want to say for the record that I am an express bus rider. I ride public transit to come to City Hall to do my work. So one thing I want to say is that, do you work closely with the NYPD around the enfor— 'cause I will tell you that most times the— where I take the bus from, because I'm in far— first of all, I'm in a transit-rich area. I happen to be lucky. But there are cars and trucks parked in the bus lane.
Yeah.
And when it come into Manhattan, it can't— they can't— you— the bus can't use the bus lane. So are you working with the NYPD to make sure there's enforcement?

Absolutely. But you know what? There's nothing like support from elected officials to help us. So, we're– you know, we do stay in close touch with them, but the hotspot that you're talking about are real and many of them are every day. We just walk outside here, just walk down–
[interposing] I know. I know.

Broadway and you see how the bus lane gets blocked. So, obviously the NYPD is fighting crime and doing a ton of things, but we welcome your help in bringing focus, consistent focus to this issue, and maybe some set-aside money in the, in the city budget for those traffic enforcement agents that are necessary. It's a separate group within
Right.
And having them funded for the dedicated purpose of keeping bus lanes open is one option that we could use your help on.

Now, I– yeah, and I appreciate that. The other thing I wanted to talk to you about, and I appreciate you're pushing, you're advancing in terms of accessibility and all of that. But, in terms of the safety, I know about the stats, but the reality is there are a lot of homeless on the— I haven't taken the subway in a long time. I'm an older adult. I have a bad— I have severe arthritis in my knees, so I can't really do that. But I hear from constituents that there are a lot of— and crime is a little different than feeling comfortable being on the train. And so, you know, there are people with mental health issues, and I understand, you know, there are things that have to be done around that as well, but I wanted to see what your sense of doing something there. And the scout teams, by the way, that the governor has are great, and it's— we could expand that. That's on the state level.
Yeah.
They work really well.

So thank you for that shout out that. The SCOUT program, just make sure

everybody's aware, is we pair a clinician with a— with several MTA police officers. Not that the police officers are dealing with the homeless person, but so that the clinician feels safe to really engage with somebody who— and this is focused only on people with severe mental illness–
[interposing] Right.

who may be candidates for, you know, involuntary commitment if they've got to come indoors for their own good or for the safety of others. So we've had that program for a couple of years now. The governor has paid to expand it. We're up to 30—
20 teams, and we're going to go to 30.

20 teams on the way to 30 teams. And we're very— overall, I don't want to waste, you know, your time, but we have seen a significant increase in customer satisfaction with safety in the subway system. I mentioned in my testimony, the highest ever stats on the feeling of safety on board trains and in the stations as well. But we got to keep pushing. You're absolutely right.

It's the one thing that's a make or break for people's willingness to ride the system.

No, absolutely. And I also wanted to ask, is there any consideration being given to expanding express buses? Because, for example, I know the express buses where I am just operate during the week. Like if they operate on the weekend, you'd have more people coming in. It's, you know, in terms of economic development and all of that and the other— so the second question to that too is that half fares, if there's any consideration. I'm going to put in a reso for half fares for the express bus, because I know in my district I have a lot of seniors who want, you know, to go to doctor's appointments, and they take it and all of that. And if there's a way to do that, that would be helpful. Okay, so fair fares gets— what? The reduced fare gets half fare on the express bus, right? Off-peak. So, let's get into– let's get into discussion. We're– the reduced fare program is hugely successful. People use it.

Right. And we, we, you know, we want to keep that constituency, but I will say this, all of our decisions, we looked at

express buses as part of the Queens bus redesign. We added one or two routes. But it's under— always under study about whether the ridership and the constituency justifies–
[interposing] Sure.
putting on a whole new route. We gotta balance the budget, but we love that express bus service seems to be really popular. The customer sat is very high.
Yes.
In the express buses.
So anyway, I'm going to try to push for half fares on the express buses.

And just to add, we did add service when congestion pricing came on. And then in addition to that, just— I think in your neck of the woods, the— what's important is this— the new city ticket where it's available all the time.
Right.
Used to be only the weekends– is a great option.
Understood.

And we have the— in Queens bus redesign, the rush routes that take you to the Long Island Railroad stations and Most recently, we now– seniors can ride in the mornings. It used to be that you had to pay a full fare.
Understood. I’m just–
[interposing] We're doing those changes. I think that might work.
I'm just going to push for that, so–
[interposing] Yeah.

And I've had conversation with the governor as well about that. I just want to— before I end, I want to give a shout out to Lucille, who works with me in my office, and she's amazing. So, thank you very much, Chair, and thank you Lieber.

You're shaming me. I should have recognized Lucille Sanghaj [sp?] who's the head of our Government Community Relations Operation and the key intermediary with so many folks in this building and City Hall.
Thank you.

Since we're on the topic of express buses, I'm just going to ask a question on that. A report found that express buses have higher average speeds but a much lower on-time reliability rate than the system overall. Many express buses travel across bridges, highways, and tunnels, allowing them to reach speeds most local buses cannot. However, they fail to reach stops at their scheduled times compared to local or SBS buses. This is problematic for riders given that express buses are less frequent than other types of service. All of the 10 bus lines with on-time performance rates below 50 percent are express buses. Are there steps that MTA has taken or could take that should improve express bus speeds on particular routes or in specific boroughs? If so, please share with the committee.

Okay, so you ask is what can MTA do? It comes back to express buses have the longest routes, so they are most subject to the impacts of all of the street conditions that we have been talking about in this hearing. So, you know, what really comes down to is, is traffic going to stop it? Is the bus lane going to be blocked? You

know, the— are the double parking going to get in the way? Will people be parked in the bus stop that makes it impossible for them to load people. All of those conditions that we need partnership with the city and more enforcement to address. Those are the reasons, the principal reasons, that express buses are more subject to delay on their much longer routes.
Thank you for answering that. I'm now going to turn it over to Council Member Wong, followed by Marte.
Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Mr. Lieber, for coming. Thank you. Before I begin, I just want to ask, do you take the bus or subway regularly?
Yes.
Okay. And how about, Sheffia [sp?]?
Shanifah.
Shanifa?
Every day.
Every day? Okay. And John?
Yeah, absolutely, every day.

Okay. That's good, that's good, because– and Jen, thank you, thank you. Okay. I really— I have really three questions. Two of them are from my constituents, and they're quite concerning. Well, I— we all grew up with OmniCards, I mean MetroCards, and every time I use it, it tells me my balance, you know, whatever. You put in $30, you know, balance $25. Or every time I do a transfer, it tells me it's transfer, three [sic]. But when I use my OmniCard, it doesn't tell me that. So my constituent who emailed me directly says, this is actually worse than the MetroCard in many ways. Can you– can you answer that? Is—
Sure.
Is something you can fix, or—

So yeah. So, right now, you can get all that kind of information at the Omni machine and you can get it online and you— there are a number of different ways. Nevertheless, I'm sympathetic to what your constituent has said. And that's why when we're— we are now trying to get over the final phase of implementing Omni, but we are already working on a variety of tools. This was all—

the Omni system in terms of software was done long before I got involved with this. And there are shortcomings and we're going to be adding customer transparency issues along the lines of what you just described.
Yeah, yeah.

So it's in process, you know, too late for some people. I'm not thrilled about those shortcomings, but the Omni system, I just wanna emphasize, has major pluses, which is if people want a weekly, they don't have to just come– reach into their pocket to see if they have $30+. They have– they can get a weekly automatically just by using it. And it's saving people $40 million in wasted money that people were investing in monthlies and weeklies a year. We're trying to save people money and give them a better deal.

Yeah, what I– but I have encountered is that constituents often felt they were overcharged and they weren't told when they used the OmniCard during transfers and only found out after the fact at the, like, at the end of the month or when they check online when they get home. Oh, I'm being charged. Why am I being charged? And then it's,

like, too late to even raise that because the person is already home.
And the— you want to talk about the customer service we do on that?

Yeah, so similar to what the chair mentioned, I mean, we have put in a lot of provisions as well as customer-facing messaging within the system. We have stood up customer service centers across the entire subway system where customers can go within their community. In the past, customers had to travel all the way downtown to Stone Street. So now we have 30 customer service centers in the boroughs that can answer these questions, as well as customers using our app. We have lots of text and email interaction, as well as, you know, good old 511. So we do have a huge customer service operation that is dedicated to this matter while we work on getting the technology for the customer-facing components.

Thank you. Yes. And again, they're so used to seeing the balance for decades. Every time you use it, you see the balance, and suddenly that feature is gone. So that is the

mindset of my constituents, and I hope you understand.
I totally get it, and we're working on it. We're going to try to improve that over time.

Thank you. My next question again is congestion pricing. My constituents, a lot of them are drivers because my district is– many parts of it is not subway accessible, so they have to drive. They're telling me that congestion is now shifted north of Manhattan, to North Manhattan, to the Bronx, and in South Brooklyn. Yes, there are fewer congestion in Lower Manhattan, but the cars are still there, still coming in. They're still leaving. What do you have to say to that?

Okay. So, I love and respect your constituents, but you're– but the data that actually has been collected publicly shows that projections about displacement of traffic, especially to the Bronx, did not turn out to be true. And there's a lot of data on that. You can go online and the New York Times did a detailed analysis of it. We had do— we have not seen, and we planned and we

analyzed that to make sure that we did— that we were ready if that did happen, and it hasn't happened as documented to date. So respectfully, I would just say, you might want to take a look at that data and share it with some of the folks who may feel otherwise.
I will look. I'm sorry, I have— Chair, may I have more time? I have one more question.
There'll be a second round.
Okay, sure. I'll ask in a second round. Thank you.
Council Member Marte, followed by Louis.
Yeah. Hey, good morning.
Good morning.

For years buses have had Omni readers at the rear door, but paying riders must board through the front. Of course, some riders still board through the back, as we all know, but they can't pay at the rear door because the Omni reader doesn't allow it. Can you tell us how much

money we're potentially losing from folks just boarding in the back and not being able to pay in the back, so that they just stay on the bus? And is there a timeline of when that back— when that rear OmniCard reader is going to go live so folks can have, you know, both front and rear door boarding?

Well, respectfully, I'd say most people are getting on the rear door, not, you know, not saying, oh gosh darn, I wish that the Omni reader were working so I could pay. They get on the back door because they know they aren't going pay there. So–
I mean, you know, maybe.

Well, let's just– let's leave that one aside for the moment. But right now, we do have– well aware that, you know, there's been a lot of discussion over the years about rear door boarding. It's not something that we're against. What we have to do is we have to reestablish the pattern of everybody's playing by the same rules when you get on the bus. It's disrespectful to the other passengers when people don't pay. And it creates an environment where, like anything in New York, we

share the public spaces. And if people aren't playing by the rules, it feels like you're a sucker if you play by the rules. And, so we get a lot of beef from our customers who say, why are so many people getting on and not paying? We— this is partly a self-created problem, honestly. We, you know, during COVID we asked everybody to get on the back, don't pay. We were trying to protect the drivers. We– toothpaste got out of the tube and we have to reestablish the principle of paying. Once we have a modern fare enforcement system where people can get on and check with a handheld validator, and that's– this year, we're going to have that. I am— once we reestablish the principle of everybody pays and expects to pay. I am willing to talk about making the backdoor a legal way to get on and pay, but we need to have that system in place, and that's coming.

Okay, thank you. You know, Council Member Schulman brought up your scout team. Is there a way to add a transparency mechanism where we can know where the scout teams have been sent? You know, there are stations in my district like the Bowery Street Station where we are constantly asking for additional support, but there's

no follow-up, there's no transparency if if folks went there, if the issues were addressed, and if they go on a routine, you know, timeline to check up on— to see if issues are a pattern or if they're one-time issues.
I’d like to get back to you on that. I, honestly, we have— obviously, we have, like, the HIPAA rules about we can't tell you about an individual.
Yeah, sure.
But I'd like to get back to you on that. John, do you have any thoughts on this?
No, we can get back to you. They're assigned by borough, so–
[interposing] yeah.
and by time of day. So the idea is that they're spread out so they're reaching a lot of different areas.
Okay.
But let's get back to you. I think there's probably some possibility that can satisfy your request.
Yeah, I think for us is mostly, you know, constituents ask. Especially there's specific subway stations that feel a little bit, you know—
[interposing] Yeah, no, and listen, we all want the folks who are suffering with severe mental illness in the public space to get help.
Yeah.

I mean, that's— this is just basic humanity. And I'm very, you know, appreciative of our riders who, you know, want to get help to some of the people, some of the neighbors they see who are struggling. So let's talk about, you know, we can share with— if we can share that information and how.

Yeah. My final question is about the Fulton Street Mall, just a few blocks away. There's been scaffolding up since 2019. My office has been asking MTA to take them down. You know, there's been a citywide campaign of shedding the sheds, and you know, it's disappointing to see that on, you know, our public lands and our public

infrastructure, we can't meet the needs of making our quality of life much better.
You're talking about the southern half of the block between Fulton and John?
Yeah, it's on 11 John Street.

Okay, so that's the old Corbin building, which is a really, really old building. I will look into that and get back to you. It's a little— you know, I'm with you, let's get the sheds down. So we'll look into that one and come back to you.
I appreciate it. Thank you for being here.
Mr. Chairman, it seems like, you know, every corner of this— of Manhattan. I'm now going to turn it over to Council Member Louis, followed by Council Member Brooks-Powers.
Thank you, Chair, and good morning–
[interposing] Good morning.

Chair Lieber. I want to echo Council Member Schulman's sentiments

about Lucille, and I want to add Shanifah in there. They've been great and very helpful. I have two quick questions, so I'm going to state the questions and then you all could jump in. I'm very happy to hear about the synergy between you and Commissioner Flynn from DOT. So I wanted to ask about Newkirk Plaza in my district. In locations where maintenance responsibilities intersect with city agencies, how does the MTA budget account for shared or disputed responsibilities? And is there any funding set aside for interagency coordination or rapid response when conditions are not addressed? And the second question is, given that then there is $9 billion allocated system-wide to repair elevated tracks and tunnels. What portion of that funding is dedicated to elevated line structures in Brooklyn, particularly the BQ right-of-way in Midwood?

Okay, so I know Newkirk Plaza. I know some of those problems, and I'm going to— I don't want to mislead you. I don't know the specifics. We don't have a general fund for, like, interagency coordination. But where there— we have real estate responsibility, we ought to have funding

to address it, and we'll come back to you with a clear answer. But, you know, I mean–
[interposing] Or you could create it.

I live on the Brighton Line. I live a couple stops north of Newkirk, so I know what you're talking about. It's got some conditions. We– listen, I'll give you the break– We will come back to you with the breakout, but the capital program that the governor got enacted in Albany last year is transformational because everybody likes new, you know, new shiny new objects. And historically there hasn't been enough investment in the existing system, which is 100 years old and falling apart. That, you know, the Bright Line, which you and I are talking about, was built like over 100 years ago to take people from, you know, the middle of Brooklyn down to Coney Island for vacations.
Right.

It really needs investment. We got the money to make those investments in the structure and those old systems. I'll give you these specific numbers, you know, as a follow-up, but that is a huge piece of our capital

program. The structures, the both above-grade structures, the ones that are in the cut like the Brighton Line–
[interposing] Right.

and also the tunnels, all of it need investment. The power systems are like the land that time forgot. And they're blowing up all the time. We keep hearing about it. There's money for that. New– you know, there is money for 2,000 new rail cars, including both 1,500 subway cars and 500 commuter rail cars. So we're getting to the stuff that has been neglected, and I'm thrilled about it. I'll give you the specific numbers in the follow-up.
I look forward to that response. Thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you, Council Member. Now we will have questions from Council Member Brooks-Powers.
